title: Hybrid Memory Cube revived: packetized cube over UCIe, no SerDes, no interposer
idea: Micron's HMC died from long-reach SerDes power (~10 pJ/bit total) and latency plus a closed consortium. Keep its smart logic base die and packet protocol, but replace the SerDes with clock-forwarded UCIe-Standard links (~0.5 pJ/bit) over a plain organic substrate at 2-10 mm reach, and publish the packet layer as an open spec so the cube becomes a drop-in memory chiplet that any accelerator can place without CoWoS.
why: HBM interposer/TSV capital and CoWoS scarcity (fact 6) plus link energy (fact 5): ~5x lower link energy than HMC, no silicon interposer, and logic-die features (ECC, repair, refresh scheduling) kept.

title: Wide I/O reborn on backside-power SoCs: memory bonded to freed frontside
idea: JEDEC Wide I/O died because ~1,200 TSVs had to pierce the hot, expensive SoC die, and phone vendors refused the yield, area and test hit. With backside power delivery (PowerVia/A16-class), the SoC's power and I/O exit through its back, so a thinned DRAM die can be hybrid-bonded face-to-face onto the SoC frontside at 3-9 um pitch with zero TSVs in either die, with refresh rate set from the logic die's thermal sensors.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): face-to-face bonds at ~0.05 pJ/bit vs ~4-5 pJ/bit for LPDDR5X, roughly 50-100x less I/O energy; removes the TSV tax (fact 6) and the package PHY area.

title: RDRAM's royalty trap fixed: royalty-free open memory-PHY commons for newcomers
idea: Rambus RDRAM lost partly because per-chip royalties, litigation and costly at-speed test made it pricier than SDRAM. Create a RISC-V-style foundation that funds, silicon-proves and licenses royalty-free DRAM-side PHYs, TSV/hybrid-bond I/O cells and controller IP, backed by a defensive patent pool of CHIPS-Act buyers, so a U.S. memory or packaging startup can tape out a base die without a $10-30M IP bill.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: removes tens of $M and months from entry, and blunts the litigation risk that killed earlier memory-interface startups.

title: FB-DIMM fixed: passive WDM optical bus, each module drops its own color
idea: FB-DIMM died because every Advanced Memory Buffer had to retime and re-drive all downstream traffic (4-6 W per DIMM, plus latency per hop). Replace the daisy chain with a motherboard waveguide carrying one wavelength per module: a passive ring filter on each module drops only its own wavelength and adds replies on a paired one, so no module repeats another's traffic and every slot sees the same latency.
why: Capacity per channel beyond DDR5's 1-2 DIMMs-per-channel electrical limit: 8-16 modules per channel at constant latency with ~5x lower buffer power than AMB, raising usable memory per socket.

title: Optane Memory Mode fixed: set-associative DRAM cache with on-controller tags
idea: Optane's Memory Mode used a direct-mapped DRAM near-memory cache, and its conflict misses made performance unpredictable, which killed adoption. Put a 16-way set-associative tag array (SRAM, ~1/512 of capacity) and a way predictor in the CXL memory controller, so a DRAM slice of 1/8 capacity fronts a cheap dense tier (NAND-backed, LPDDR or retired DDR4) with predictable miss rates under 5%.
why: Do DRAM's job with less: cuts DRAM bits per server 4-8x for capacity-bound workloads while keeping ~90-95% of all-DRAM performance, directly offsetting the 4x price spike.

title: US Memories 2.0: binding take-or-pay buyers for a U.S. HBM-stacking plant
idea: The 1989 U.S. Memories consortium (IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed in January 1990 because members would not sign purchase obligations once DRAM prices fell. Re-run it for the back end only (TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, base-die attach and test of HBM/CXL modules from known-good DRAM wafers bought globally), with binding 7-year take-or-pay contracts under a price collar and a federal buyer of last resort feeding a strategic memory reserve.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: a stacking/test plant costs ~$2-4B vs $15B+ for a front-end fab and captures the HBM TSV/packaging bottleneck (fact 6); the contracts remove the price-cycle risk that killed the original.

title: Sun Proximity Communication fixed by capillary self-alignment and electronic pad steering
idea: Sun's capacitive face-to-face proximity communication died because overlapping chips needed micron-level alignment and gap control that packaging could not hold. Place DRAM tiles over logic tiles by water-droplet capillary self-assembly (hydrophilic landing sites give <1 um placement), set the gap with oxide standoffs, and oversample each signal with a 3x3 cluster of transmit micro-pads from which the receiver picks the best-aligned one at boot: no solder, no TSVs, reworkable tiles.
why: Data movement and the HBM TSV tax: ~0.1 pJ/bit capacitive links at 10-20 um pitch with no bonding yield loss; reworkable tiles remove stack-yield multiplication (fact 6, 20-30% loss).

title: ThruChip inductive stacking fixed: coils in top metal over cell arrays
idea: Keio's ThruChip Interface (inductive coupling between stacked dies) never shipped because its coils ate die area and power still needed TSVs, so nothing was saved. Draw the transmit/receive coils in the DRAM's top metal directly above the cell arrays, where that level is otherwise lightly used, carry data inductively through all thinned dies, and keep only a few hundred coarse-pitch (50-100 um) power TSVs that are cheap and high-yield.
why: Removes the thousands of fine-pitch data TSVs behind HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield loss (fact 6): ~10-15% die area recovered and stack yield closer to single-die yield.

title: Mercury delay line reborn: fiber-loop memory circulating AI weights at light speed
idea: Delay-line memory died because data was only available as it came round (sequential access) and the medium drifted with temperature. LLM inference reads every weight in the same order each token, so sequential access is fine: a ~10 km multicore-fiber loop (19 cores x C+L WDM, ~1 Pb/s) holds several GB in flight with all-optical amplifiers and a clock-recovering regenerator every few laps, and taps feed each accelerator as its layer's weights come round.
why: HBM capacity and data movement (facts 5, 6): weights delivered at ~100 TB/s with holding cost set by amplifier power (tens of W) rather than DRAM bits, freeing HBM for KV cache; claimed 2-5x less HBM for weight-streaming inference.

title: Automata Processor fixed: one hard-wired in-DRAM job, KV-cache top-k filtering
idea: Micron's Automata Processor died because nobody wanted to program NFAs and DRAM-process logic was slow. Hard-wire one function with a huge market: each bank's sense-amp stripe computes 4-bit dot products of a broadcast query against the open row of keys and returns only the indices of the top-k matches, so the accelerator fetches just those KV entries through one new command and no programming model.
why: Overfetch and data movement (facts 5, 8): long-context attention moves 10-30x less KV data off-chip, using bank-level parallelism for TB/s internal bandwidth.

title: IRAM fixed: leading-edge logic hybrid-bonded under every DRAM subarray
idea: Berkeley IRAM, Venray TOMI and UPMEM stalled because logic built in a DRAM process is 3-10x slower and wire-starved (about 3 metal layers). Wafer-to-wafer hybrid-bond (<1 um pitch) a 5 nm logic wafer face-to-face to a DRAM array wafer stripped of most periphery, so each 512-row subarray gets its own decoders, sense-adjacent SIMD lane and controller in fast CMOS directly beneath it.
why: Periphery at 49% of the die (fact 7) moves to the logic wafer, giving ~1.6-1.8x more cells per DRAM wafer; near-memory compute at ~0.1 pJ/bit with 10-100x the external bandwidth.

title: Xeon Phi capacity limit fixed: DRAM stacks on package underside too
idea: Knights Landing's on-package MCDRAM was abandoned largely because 16 GB was too small, a ceiling set by package beachfront beside the die. Use a glass-core substrate with 25-50 um through-glass vias to mount a second ring of memory stacks on the package underside, directly beneath the processor's I/O edge, with a board cutout and bottom cold plate, doubling the stacks within ~5 mm of the PHY.
why: Breaks the beachfront limit on stacks per accelerator: ~2x on-package capacity at the same short-reach pJ/bit, delaying the need for far memory.

title: Refurbished-RAM trade died of test cost; PUF-certified reuse DRAM tier
idea: Secondary-market DRAM never scaled because per-module retest cost and counterfeit risk made buyers distrust it. Harvest DIMMs from decommissioned servers onto CXL expander cards whose controller runs full march and retention tests in situ and reads each die's retention-failure map as a physically unclonable fingerprint, issuing a signed provenance and health certificate, then sell the result as a 'certified reuse' capacity tier.
why: Raises usable memory supply with no new fab capital: millions of retired DIMMs a year re-enter service as a slower capacity tier, blunting the 4x price spike.

title: Tezzaron wafer-stack yield fixed: spare tier plus base-die remap
idea: Tezzaron's wafer-on-wafer DRAM stacks struggled because stack yield is the product of tier yields, with no way to drop a bad tier after bonding. Stack N+1 tiers (e.g., 9 for 8), each tier's TSV bus independently gated by fuse-programmed switches in the base die; post-bond test finds the worst tier and the base die routes around it, and when all tiers are good the extra one is sold as capacity.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6): multiplicative yield becomes 'any 8 of 9', lifting good-stack yield from ~75% to ~95% for ~11% more DRAM silicon, and makes cheaper wafer-on-wafer bonding viable.

title: MCM known-good-die curse fixed: contactless near-field wafer test
idea: 1990s multichip modules died of the known-good-die problem, and HBM repeats it because hybrid-bond pads cannot be touched by probe needles (scratches ruin bonding), so dies are bonded half-tested. Add a field of tiny capacitive/inductive near-field couplers in top metal and test each DRAM wafer at full speed, including burn-in and retention, through a matching contactless probe card before any bonding.
why: HBM stack yield (fact 6) and capital: full at-speed known-good-die screening could recover most of the 20-30% stack loss and the scrapped base dies, for <0.5% die area.

title: Trilogy's wafer-scale dream fixed: an unsawn DRAM wafer as memory backplane
idea: Gene Amdahl's Trilogy failed on wafer-scale yield and on CTE-driven delamination between the wafer and its packaging. Keep a whole 300 mm DRAM wafer unsawn (~3-4 TB raw at ~0.4 Gb/mm2), map out bad reticles at test, and hybrid-bond logic chiplets face-to-face only onto good reticle sites; because everything is silicon on silicon there is no CTE mismatch, and dicing, packaging, TSVs and interposers disappear.
why: Removes package, TSV and interposer cost (fact 6) and data-movement energy (~0.05 pJ/bit face-to-face): TB-class memory at on-die bandwidth, with a claimed 30-50% lower cost per delivered GB than HBM.

title: Z-RAM revived as a bonded cache tile, sense amps in logic below
idea: Innovative Silicon's capacitorless floating-body Z-RAM died because it required SOI logic wafers and its sense margin collapsed under logic-process variation, so AMD dropped it. Build the floating-body array alone on its own SOI chiplet, with no compromise to the CPU process, and hybrid-bond it over a logic die that holds low-offset, auto-zeroed sense amplifiers and refresh logic for every 64 kb tile at 1-2 um bond pitch.
why: Avoids the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the TSV tax: a capacitorless near-memory tier at ~2-3x SRAM density with face-to-face bandwidth that absorbs external DRAM traffic.

title: KryoTech fixed: hermetic Peltier-cooled DRAM tile trades refresh for density
idea: KryoTech's sub-ambient PC cooling (1990s) died on condensation and compressor cost. Cool only the low-power DRAM stack (a few W) to ~20 C with a thin-film thermoelectric inside a hermetically sealed dry-nitrogen package cavity while the logic stays at 85-100 C. Retention roughly doubles every ~10 C, so the tens-of-times longer retention can be spent on less refresh or a 30-40% smaller storage capacitor.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and the capacitor wall (fact 1): refresh energy and bandwidth loss largely eliminated, or Cs relaxed for lower-aspect-ratio, cheaper etch, at ~1-3 W of Peltier power per stack.

title: CCD memory reborn as charge-packet data bus inside DRAM periphery
idea: 1970s CCD memories lost to DRAM because serial shifting made random access slow, yet moving charge packets down a buried channel is extremely cheap per hop. Use a short CCD-style bucket-brigade channel to carry the 128-256 bits fetched from a bank toward the I/O hub as charge packets clocked at ~0.3 V, instead of full-swing global I/O lines, serializing the data naturally as it moves.
why: On-die data movement (facts 5, 8): global I/O wiring is a large share of DRAM read energy; claimed 2-4x lower on-die transport energy per bit and fewer long metal lines in the periphery (fact 7).

title: Wireless NoC fixed: sealed package cavity broadcasts DRAM commands at 300 GHz
idea: On-chip wireless networks died because tiny antennas radiated poorly into lossy silicon and multipath was unpredictable. Make the package lid and substrate a sealed metal cavity tuned as a 300 GHz waveguide, so on-die antennas on every DRAM die and the controller share a predictable, low-loss broadcast medium for command/address and clock (low-rate, all-to-all), while data stays on wires.
why: Removes command/address TSVs, wires and fan-out buffers in stacks and modules (facts 6, 7), so dies can be added without rerouting; claimed 10-20% fewer TSVs and lower C/A power.

title: IBM MXT fixed: compression lives in the CXL link, not the core
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled effective capacity with hardware compression but died from decompression latency on the CPU critical path, a large L3 requirement and OS changes. Put a 2-4 ns base-delta/zero-run compressor with a metadata cache inside the CXL memory controller, present the OS a fixed larger capacity, and compress only far-tier lines so hot data never pays the latency.
why: Do DRAM's job with less, and link energy: server data typically compresses 1.5-2.5x, so 33-60% fewer DRAM bits for the same capacity and fewer bits crossing the link.

title: Asynchronous logic fixed: clockless 1-of-4 links inside the HBM stack
idea: Asynchronous design (Fulcrum, Handshake Solutions) failed because whole-chip async needed tools nobody had. Confine it to one hard IP block: the vertical links between HBM core dies and the base die use delay-insensitive 1-of-4 encoding with completion detection, so the stack needs no clock TSVs, DLLs or per-die clock trees and each die runs as fast as its process corner allows.
why: Data movement (fact 5): clock distribution and DLLs are ~20-40% of DRAM I/O power and standby current; removing them and their timing margins claims 25-35% lower in-stack I/O energy and better yield across corners.

title: Virtual Channel SDRAM revived: sector caches and sub-row activation in base die
idea: NEC's VC-SDRAM put SRAM channel buffers in each DRAM to cut row conflicts, but died because its 3-5% die-area cost was too much for a commodity part and controllers ignored it. In HBM/CXL stacks the logic base die offers cheap area: give it per-bank 64 B sector caches and drive segmented wordlines so only the 1/8 row segment holding the requested sector activates, returning sectors instead of whole pages.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): 8x fewer cells activated per random access, cutting the ~5.9 pJ per useful bit by ~3-5x, and fewer full-row activations ease row hammer (fact 9).

title: Cu-Mn self-forming barrier, failed in fine lines, revived for TSVs
idea: Cu-Mn alloy seeds that self-form a MnSiO barrier on anneal were dropped from advanced BEOL because residual Mn raised resistivity in 20 nm lines, a penalty that vanishes in 2-10 um TSVs, hybrid-bond pads and contact plugs. Use Cu-0.5%Mn seed in HBM TSVs, hybrid-bond pads and base-die contact plugs to eliminate Ta/TaN barriers and W plugs; the 2-3 nm self-formed barrier also frees TSV diameter.
why: Removes Ta (conflict-region supply) and W (China ~80%) from the memory interconnect stack and cuts PVD steps (capital) and TSV stress; Cu and Mn only.

title: CNT vias failed on growth heat; transfer-grow iron-catalyzed CNT TSVs instead
idea: Carbon-nanotube vias (Fujitsu, imec) never reached production because good CNTs need ~700 C growth, incompatible with BEOL, and tip contact resistance was high. Grow dense vertical CNT forests from an Fe/Al2O3 catalyst (no Co) on a sacrificial carrier, transfer them into etched TSV holes with polymer fill, then Cu-plate the exposed tips, so the via is carbon in the barrel and Cu only at the contacts.
why: TSV CTE stress: CNT's near-zero CTE shrinks the transistor keep-out zone around each TSV ~3-5x, recovering die area lost to the HBM TSV tax (fact 6); no W or Co, ~100x Cu ampacity.

title: Zinc solders abandoned for corrosion; Zn-Al fluxless joints inside sealed stacks
idea: Sn-Zn and Zn-Al solders were rejected in the 2006 lead-free transition because Zn oxidizes and corrodes in humid, flux-based board assembly. Inside an HBM-style stack the joint is never exposed: deposit Zn-Al eutectic caps on Cu pillars, reflow fluxless in formic-acid vapor and encapsulate immediately in molded underfill, replacing SnAg microbumps and In-based low-temperature solders.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes Sn (~2 ppm of the crust, concentrated supply), Ag and In from the microbump layer of every stack; Zn-Al (381 C) also serves as a high-temperature first joint in the solder hierarchy.

title: ACF failed at fine pitch; magnetically aligned iron-nickel columns fix shorts
idea: Anisotropic conductive films lost to solder at fine pitch because randomly dispersed particles bridged neighbors or missed pads. Disperse Ni-coated Fe microspheres in epoxy and cure under a vertical magnetic field so they self-assemble into isolated columns at ~10 um pitch, giving a solderless, reworkable vertical interconnect for attaching memory stacks or tiles to substrates.
why: Solder-free (no Sn, Ag, In or Au) and reworkable: a bad memory stack can be replaced instead of scrapping a $1,000+ accelerator package, attacking HBM assembly yield (fact 6).

title: Silicon LEDs failed on efficiency; SPAD receivers make them enough
idea: Silicon light emitters were abandoned for links because indirect-gap emission is 1e-5 efficient or worse. Across bonded dies (<20 um of oxide), a receiver built from silicon single-photon avalanche diodes needs only ~20-50 photons per bit, so a reverse-biased avalanche-mode Si junction, emitting fast 600-900 nm hot-carrier light, can signal die-to-die with no III-V, Ge or In.
why: Data movement with zero banned elements: a contactless, crosstalk-free optical die-to-die link needing no bumps; ~1-5 pJ/bit at first, limited honestly by emitter efficiency.

title: Iron-disilicide LED fizzled; Purcell microcavity makes it a 1.55-um source
idea: Surrey's 1997 beta-FeSi2 light-emitting diode on silicon faded because room-temperature emission was weak. Embed FeSi2 nanocrystals in a silicon photonic-crystal nanocavity (Q ~1e4) to Purcell-enhance the radiative rate 10-50x, couple straight into Si waveguides, and detect with divacancy-implanted silicon waveguide photodiodes, giving an in-package photonic memory link with no InP, GaAs, Ge or Er.
why: Data movement and scarce resources: replaces III-V lasers (Ga, In) and Ge detectors in co-packaged memory optics, targeting <2 pJ/bit with fully Earth-abundant photonics (Fe, Si, O).

title: Optical clock trees failed on alignment; a light shaft through the stack
idea: Free-space optical clock distribution (1980s-2000s research) failed because external optics could not stay aligned to chips. Etch one 20-50 um oxide-lined vertical hole through every die of a memory stack so it acts as a light pipe, put an n-ZnO/p-NiO UV LED in the base die at its bottom, and let a ring photodiode on each die's shaft wall tap the pulse, broadcasting clock and command strobes to all tiers with sub-ps skew.
why: Removes clock/strobe TSVs and per-tier deskew circuits (fact 6), shrinking in-stack timing margins and power; uses only Zn, Ni, O and Si.

title: Keyssa's contactless connector failed in phones; it fits gold-free memory modules
idea: Keyssa's 60 GHz near-field 'kiss' connectors failed commercially because phone connectors were cheap and good enough. Server memory slots are now the signal-integrity wall at DDR5-8800+ and use gold-plated contacts, so replace the DIMM edge connector with an array of CMOS 60-140 GHz near-field couplers with plain Cu antennas, giving a sealed, wear-free, hot-swappable module interface.
why: Removes Au contact plating and connector wear failures; contactless lanes at ~1-2 pJ/bit allow faster modules and more slots per channel, raising capacity per socket.

title: Sub-THz plastic waveguides lost to optics; In/Ga bans flip that
idea: Polymer dielectric waveguides carrying 100-300 GHz carriers lost to optical cables because lasers were cheaper at volume. With In/Ga-based lasers ruled out, use solid polyethylene or PTFE ribbons fed by CMOS sub-THz transceivers to connect compute sleds to memory sleds at 1-3 m, carrying 100+ Gb/s per ribbon at ~1-2 pJ/bit with no lasers.
why: Rack-scale memory pooling reclaims the 20-30% of server DRAM that sits stranded, without lasers that need In or Ga; materials are C, H, F, Si and Cu.

title: Silicon-on-AlN failed on bonding; AlN as hybrid-bond dielectric spreads heat
idea: Silicon-on-aluminum-nitride SOI, meant to cure self-heating, died because rough AlN bonded poorly. Hybrid-bond interfaces need only a few hundred nm of dielectric: deposit smooth amorphous AlN (~10-30 W/m-K vs ~1.4 for SiO2) capped with 10 nm of SiCN for bonding chemistry, so every HBM tier gets a lateral heat-spreading plane at each bond line.
why: Thermal limits on taller, faster stacks: claimed 10-20 C lower core-die peaks, fewer refresh-rate doublings (fact 3) and room for more tiers; Al, N, Si and C only.

title: SrTiO3 DRAM capacitors failed on leakage; decaps tolerate it
idea: Strontium titanate (k ~100-300) was abandoned for DRAM storage capacitors because its leakage was far too high for fA-level retention and it wanted Ru electrodes. Power decoupling tolerates ~1000x more leakage, so deposit STO on TiN electrodes in deep trenches of the interposer or base die for several-uF/mm2 decaps that steady ultra-wide I/O supplies, replacing Ta capacitors and Hf/Zr-oxide MIMs.
why: Lets HBM-class I/O run at lower VDDQ with thinner noise margins (facts 5, 10) and removes Ta, Hf and Ru from memory power delivery; Sr, Ti, O and N only.

title: Copper-sinter pastes failed from oxidation; formate copper replaces indium TIM
idea: Copper nanoparticle sinter pastes lost to silver sinter because Cu oxidized and needed hydrogen furnaces. Use Cu-formate complex inks that decompose in situ at ~200 C into fresh, oxide-free Cu, sintering a 20-50 um porous Cu layer between HBM/accelerator dies and the lid in place of indium solder and gallium liquid-metal thermal interfaces.
why: Removes In and Ga from the TIM of >700 W accelerator packages; sintered Cu (~100-200 W/m-K vs ~80 for In) keeps memory stacks cooler for more bandwidth and less refresh.

title: Core memory's ferrite returns: transformer-coupled power through the stack
idea: Magnetic core memory died of hand-threaded cores, but its ferrites are cheap Earth-abundant flux guides. Spin-spray-plate thin-film MnZn-ferrite cores through ~30 um holes in each thinned DRAM die, with a primary winding in the base die and secondary spirals on each tier, and transfer power magnetically at ~50-100 MHz so power TSVs and their keep-out zones disappear; paired with contactless data links, the stack becomes TSV-free.
why: Removes the power TSVs that block TSV-free stacking (fact 6, ~5-10% die area) and isolates supply noise per tier; Fe, Mn, Zn, O and Cu only, no Co-based magnetics.

title: Intel FIVR retreated; Sendust inductors in glass give per-channel memory DVFS
idea: Intel pulled its fully integrated voltage regulator after Haswell/Broadwell because air-core package inductors were lossy and hot, and the research magnetic inductors used banned CoZrTa. Embed laminated, sputtered Sendust (Fe-Si-Al) inductors in a glass-core substrate under each memory stack to feed per-channel buck converters in the base die, so each HBM/LPDDR channel scales VDDQ and VDD in 25 mV steps with load.
why: Voltage floor and CV2 energy (facts 5, 10): per-channel DVFS can cut I/O and array energy 20-35% during low-utilization phases; magnetics use only Fe, Si and Al.

title: Charge-recycling buses failed on imbalance; balanced coding fixes voltage-stacked HBM lanes
idea: Charge-recycling (voltage-stacked) buses from 1990s research failed because data-dependent current imbalance between stacked lane groups collapsed the mid-rail. Split a 1,024-bit HBM bus into two stacked groups (0-0.4 V and 0.4-0.8 V) so charge spent by the upper group powers the lower, and apply DC-balanced 8b/9b-style coding per group so transitions match each cycle, leaving only a tiny mid-rail regulator.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~2x lower I/O energy by reusing each coulomb, and balanced current shrinks the decoupling needed (fewer Ta/Hf decaps); plain Si CMOS and Cu.

title: MEMS relay computers died of contact wear; relays pool memory instead
idea: Berkeley-style MEMS relay logic failed because contacts wore out within ~1e9 cycles and switched too slowly for logic. Memory pooling switches only when allocations change (minutes), so build an in-package crossbar of electrostatic poly-Si relays with TiN/carbon contacts (no Ru, Pt or W) that physically re-wires memory chiplets between compute dies, with zero standby power and no SerDes.
why: Stranded memory: package- or board-level DRAM follows whichever die needs it, reclaiming 15-30% stranded capacity with no added latency once connected; Si, Ti, N and C only.

title: X-Celeprint transfer printing failed in displays; print DRAM dielets onto logic
idea: Micro-transfer printing (X-Celeprint/X Display) stalled because displays needed millions of microLEDs placed at six-sigma yield. Memory needs only tens to hundreds of large dielets per wafer: undercut-release 5-10 um thick DRAM dielets, pick them in parallel with PDMS stamps onto a logic wafer, and connect them with one lithographic Cu/Al redistribution layer over the planarized surface, with no bumps, solder or TSVs.
why: Removes microbump solder (Sn, Ag, In) and TSVs (fact 6), selects known-good dielets, and gives 2-5 um RDL pitch at ~0.1 pJ/bit; Si, O, C, Cu and Al only.

title: Acoustic delay lines died; AlN ultrasound carries data through stacked dies
idea: Acoustic delay-line memories died of sequential access, yet they proved GHz acoustic waves travel cleanly through solids. Put thin-film AlN bulk-acoustic transducers with Al/TiN electrodes (no Sc or Mo) on each thinned DRAM die so 5-10 GHz acoustic pulses cross the bonded silicon stack vertically, and phase a transducer array per channel to beam-steer to the target tier, giving a TSV-free, wire-free vertical data path.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): vertical data without TSVs or coils, relying on low GHz acoustic loss in Si; claimed 10-50 Gb/s per transducer cluster using Al, N, Ti and Si only.

title: Spectrum-sliced LED WDM failed in telecom; incandescent silicon sources suit packages
idea: Spectrum-sliced incoherent WDM (one broadband source cut into channels) died in telecom from excess intensity noise and low power per slice over km distances. Over 1-10 mm in-package paths, a microheated SiC/silicon photonic-crystal selective thermal emitter (W-free) can feed SiN waveguides whose silicon microrings slice and modulate dozens of channels, detected by Si photodiodes below 1.1 um, with no laser at all.
why: Removes III-V lasers (Ga, In), the dominant cost and failure item in co-packaged optics, from memory links; ~5 pJ/bit at first with a path toward ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Lead-free's chaotic transition fixed: shared qualification bank for abundant materials
idea: The 2006 RoHS lead-free switch went badly (tin whiskers, brittle joints) because each OEM repeated years of reliability testing alone. Fund a pre-competitive U.S. qualification bank, CHIPS-funded and governed by OSATs and hyperscalers, that runs JEDEC thermal-cycle, electromigration and HAST tests once on Earth-abundant packaging materials (Zn-Al joints, Cu-Mn barriers, Cu sinter, AlN dielectrics, ferrite magnetics) and publishes shared data and design rules.
why: Cuts 2-3 years and per-firm cost from qualification, making substitution away from Sn, Ag, In, Ta, W and Co practical for U.S. memory packaging and resilient to chokepoints.

title: Computational sprinting's wax died; salt-hydrate buffers let HBM burst bandwidth
idea: Computational sprinting (UPenn, 2012) proposed paraffin heat buffers but never shipped because wax conducts poorly and re-solidifies slowly. Fill the spacer and dummy-die volumes beside HBM stacks with magnesium nitrate hexahydrate (melts ~89 C, ~160 J/g) infiltrated into sealed copper foam, which soaks up heat right at HBM's throttle point so stacks can run 20-40% higher bandwidth for tens of seconds and re-freeze during idle phases.
why: Thermal throttling and temperature-doubled refresh (fact 3) during AI bursts, letting a smaller memory system meet peak demand; Mg, N, O, H and Cu only.

title: Cyclos resonant clocking dropped over DVFS; memory strobes run fixed frequency
idea: Cyclos' resonant clock mesh shipped in AMD Piledriver and then vanished because on-die inductors cost area and resonance broke across wide DVFS frequency ranges. Memory interfaces run a fixed frequency per speed bin on heavily loaded clock/strobe (WCK/DQS) networks, so resonate those networks with air-core Cu inductors in the package RDL or interposer (no Co/Fe magnetics, no die area), recovering ~50-70% of their CV2 energy each cycle.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): clock/strobe toggling is ~20-30% of memory PHY power, so a claimed 10-20% total PHY energy cut using only Cu and dielectric.

title: OSP finishes failed after reflows; graphene/h-BN monolayers replace ENEPIG gold
idea: Organic solderability preservatives were the cheap alternative to Ni/Pd/Au (ENEPIG) pad finishes but failed because they degrade after multiple reflows, which multi-die memory packages need. Coat Cu substrate pads with a transferred or low-temperature plasma-grown monolayer of graphene or h-BN that blocks oxidation through repeated 260 C cycles yet is thin enough for Cu-Cu or Zn-Al joints to break through during bonding.
why: Removes Pd and Au from every memory package substrate pad, cutting BOM and precious-metal supply risk; C, B and N only.
